title: The Day a Computer Beat the World Chess Champion
description:
In May 1997, IBM's Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match. Kasparov accused IBM of cheating. IBM retired the machine instead of giving him a rematch.

This is the story of the first time a computer beat the best human player alive at the game that had stood for human intelligence for centuries: how Deep Blue worked, the move that rattled Kasparov, and why it was a very different kind of AI from the ones we use today.

segments.say: On May the eleventh, 1997, in a room in New York, the world chess champion resigned after just nineteen moves, stood up, and walked away from the board.
His opponent wasn't a person. It was a computer built by IBM, called Deep Blue. And with that game, it won the match.

For centuries, chess had stood for human intelligence itself. That afternoon, a machine beat the best human player alive. This is how it happened, and why it mattered less, and more, than people thought.
Since the very start of computing, researchers saw chess as the perfect test for machine intelligence. The rules are simple, the results are clear, and being good at it seemed to need real thought.
The problem is size. The number of possible chess games is so large that no computer could ever check them all. So a chess program has to search the moves that matter and judge the rest.
For decades, programs got steadily stronger. By the late 1980s they could beat strong club players. But the world champion was another matter.
That champion was Garry Kasparov. He became world champion in 1985 at twenty-two, the youngest ever at the time, and he was widely seen as one of the strongest players in history.
Kasparov was aggressive, fiercely prepared, and confident he could out-think any machine. For a while, he was right.
Deep Blue began as a student project at Carnegie Mellon University in the mid-1980s, led by Feng-hsiung Hsu, who designed a chip built for one job: chess. IBM hired the team, and the project grew.
The 1997 version ran on an IBM supercomputer with hundreds of those custom chess chips working together. It could examine around two hundred million positions every second.
But speed alone wasn't enough. Deep Blue also had a way of scoring positions, written by its team with help from chess grandmasters. Thousands of hand-tuned rules about pieces, pawns and king safety.
That's important. Deep Blue didn't learn chess the way modern AI learns. People told it what good chess looked like, and it searched faster than any human ever could.

The first match was in Philadelphia in February 1996. In game one, Deep Blue won. It was the first time a computer had beaten a reigning world champion in a game played at normal tournament time limits.
Then Kasparov adapted. He steered games into slow, strategic positions where the machine had less to calculate, and he won the match four games to two.
IBM spent the next year upgrading the machine, and asked for a rematch.
The rematch began in New York in May 1997. Six games, with the whole world watching. Kasparov won the first game.
In game two, Deep Blue played quiet, patient moves that looked strangely human. It avoided grabbing material that most programs of the time would have taken. Kasparov was rattled, and resigned.
Afterwards, analysts found that in the final position, Kasparov could have forced a draw. He had resigned a game he didn't need to lose.
Kasparov suspected something. He said the machine's play in game two was too deep, too human, and hinted that people might have stepped in during the game. IBM denied it.
He asked to see Deep Blue's printouts, its record of what it was thinking. IBM didn't hand them over during the match. Some were published later, and no evidence of human help was ever shown.
But the damage was done. The next three games were draws. Kasparov looked tired and suspicious, playing the machine as if it might be hiding something.
In game six, Kasparov made an early mistake in a well-known opening. Deep Blue sacrificed a knight, broke open his position, and within nineteen moves, it was over.
Deep Blue won the match three and a half to two and a half. For the first time, a computer had beaten the world champion over a full match.

Kasparov wanted another rematch. IBM declined, and retired the machine. One of its two towers went to the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, and the other to the Computer History Museum in California.
There's a twist. Years later, one of Deep Blue's designers, Murray Campbell, told the writer Nate Silver that a strange move near the end of the first game was caused by a bug.
The machine couldn't decide, so it played a fallback move. According to that account, Kasparov may have read deep meaning into it, and the doubt stayed with him for the rest of the match.
If that's right, it's a very human story. We see intention in machines, even when there's none there. It's the same instinct people had with ELIZA, back in episode two.
So, was Deep Blue intelligent? Its own creators were careful about that. It was a brilliant feat of engineering. But it couldn't learn, and it couldn't do anything except play chess.
Compare that with AlphaGo, from episode one. Nineteen years later, AlphaGo learned Go largely by itself, from data and self-play, instead of following rules written by people.
Those are the two big paths in AI history. Tell the machine the rules and let it search. Or let the machine learn the rules for itself. Today's chatbots come from the second path.
And Kasparov? He didn't turn against computers. A year later, he helped launch a new kind of chess, sometimes called advanced chess, where humans play with a computer helping them.
He argued that a person working with a machine could beat either one alone. Twenty years later, he wrote a book about it, called Deep Thinking.
And chess didn't die. Today, programs on a phone can beat any human, and more people play chess than ever. Players use computers to train, to prepare, and to understand the game better.
Deep Blue didn't prove machines could think. It proved something narrower, and just as important. With enough engineering, a machine could beat the best human at a task we thought needed a mind.
That pattern has repeated ever since. Chess, then Go, then images, then language. Each time, we say that's not real intelligence. And each time, the line moves.
That's AI Turning Points. Next, the experiment run from a bedroom that started today's AI boom. Subscribe so you don't miss it.

title: The Bedroom Experiment That Started the AI Boom
description:
In 2012, a graduate student trained a neural network on two gaming graphics cards and smashed the world's biggest image recognition contest. Within a year, the tech giants were in a bidding war for him and his professor.

This is the story of ImageNet and AlexNet: the dataset nobody wanted to fund, the model that crushed the competition, and how a pair of graphics cards turned deep learning into the engine of modern AI.

segments.say: In 2012, a graduate student in Toronto trained a computer program on two graphics cards, the kind people bought for video games. He ran it from his bedroom.
That program entered the world's biggest contest for recognising images, and it didn't just win. It beat the second-best entry by a margin nobody in the field had seen before.
Within a year, the biggest tech companies on Earth were bidding for the team. Many researchers now point to that moment as the start of today's AI boom. This is how it happened.
Recognising what's in a photo feels effortless for us. A cat, a car, a cup of coffee. For computers, it was one of the hardest problems in AI.
For years, researchers tried to write rules. Look for edges, look for shapes, look for these patterns. It worked a little, but real photos are messy, and the rules kept breaking.

Another idea was to let the computer learn from examples, using neural networks, systems loosely inspired by the brain. The idea was decades old, but it had a reputation for not working on big problems.
Then a young computer scientist named Fei-Fei Li made a bet. She thought the missing piece wasn't a cleverer program. It was data. Far more examples than anyone had ever collected.
Starting around 2007, her team began building ImageNet, a database of photos, each labelled with what it showed. Many colleagues thought it was a waste of time.
To label that many images, they used Amazon Mechanical Turk, paying thousands of online workers around the world to sort pictures. ImageNet eventually grew to more than fourteen million images.
In 2010, they launched a yearly contest. Teams trained programs on more than a million labelled photos across a thousand categories, then were tested on images they'd never seen.
For the first two years, results improved slowly. The best systems still got the answer wrong about a quarter of the time, even when allowed five guesses.

At the University of Toronto, Geoffrey Hinton had spent decades working on neural networks, through years when much of the field had moved on. His students thought ImageNet was the chance to prove the idea.
One student, Alex Krizhevsky, built the network. Another, Ilya Sutskever, pushed him to try ImageNet. Hinton supervised. The model would become known as AlexNet.
The key was graphics cards. GPUs are built to do huge numbers of simple calculations at once, for video games. That turns out to be exactly what training a neural network needs.
Krizhevsky wrote software to train the network on two gaming GPUs, running in his bedroom at his parents' house. Training took about a week.
When the 2012 results came in, AlexNet's error rate, with five guesses, was fifteen point three percent. The next best entry was twenty-six point two percent.
In a contest where teams fought over a percentage point or two, that was enormous. Neural networks hadn't just caught up. They'd jumped ahead.

The network had about sixty million adjustable numbers. It used a few tricks that are now standard, like randomly switching off parts of the network during training, so it couldn't just memorise the photos.
The field changed almost overnight. Within a couple of years, nearly every top entry in the contest used deep neural networks.
Hinton and his two students formed a tiny company. In 2013, several tech giants bid for it in a private auction. Google won, reportedly for about forty-four million dollars.
Progress kept accelerating. By 2015, a Microsoft system got the error rate down to about three and a half percent. A researcher who tested himself on the same task had scored about five percent.
But ImageNet also taught a harder lesson. A model learns whatever is in its data, including the mistakes and biases of the people who labelled it.
In 2019, researchers and artists highlighted offensive and biased labels in ImageNet's categories for people. The ImageNet team removed a large share of those images and tightened its rules.
The same problem is everywhere in AI today. A model is only as fair as the data it learned from.
The people in this story went on to shape modern AI. Ilya Sutskever co-founded OpenAI in 2015. Fei-Fei Li kept leading research on computer vision and AI policy.
And in 2024, Geoffrey Hinton shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with John Hopfield, for foundational work that made machine learning with neural networks possible.
The graphics card became the engine of the boom. The same kind of chip that ran AlexNet now powers the data centres behind today's chatbots, just in vastly larger numbers.
AlexNet showed that three things together could change everything: lots of data, enough computing power, and neural networks big enough to use both.
That recipe hasn't really changed. The transformer from episode three made it work for language. Then companies scaled it up, and up again.
That's AI Turning Points. If you want more stories like this, subscribe. And to see how that recipe learned to write, go back to episode three, the paper with a joke title.
